title: Narrative syntax, and Aramaic beside Hebrew

objectives.can: Follow an Aramaic narrative: perfects and participles linked by אֱדַיִן and בֵּאדַיִן, with no wayyiqtol; and name the main differences from Hebrew syntax.

explanation.summary: Hebrew stories run on a special narrative verb, the wayyiqtol. Biblical Aramaic has no such form. Its stories run on ordinary perfects and participles, joined by וְ and marked as steps by the adverbs אֱדַיִן and בֵּאדַיִן, 'then'. This lesson follows one story, Daniel 3:19–25, and then sets Aramaic and Hebrew side by side.

sections.heading: No consecutive forms
body: In Biblical Hebrew a story is usually told with the wayyiqtol: a verb with a prefix וַ and an imperfect-type form, which carries the action forward in time ('and he said', 'and he answered'). A matching form with the perfect, the weqatal, does something similar for repeated or future action. These are called consecutive forms.

The Aramaic of the Bible has neither. If you ask the analysed texts for every verb form, the list is perfect, imperfect, participle, passive participle, imperative and infinitive, and nothing else. A story in Aramaic uses these ordinary forms. וְ still means 'and' or 'but', and it still joins clauses, but it does not change the verb into a narrative tense and it does not by itself say that one event followed another.

sections.heading: A story told with perfects and participles
body: Read Daniel 3:19–25. The king's anger is told with perfects: בֵּאדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר הִתְמְלִי חֱמָא ... אֶשְׁתַּנִּי, 'then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury… (his face) was changed'. His speech begins with the pair עָנֵה וְאָמַר, two participles. The orders are carried out in perfects joined by וְ: in 3:21 גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ כְּפִתוּ ... וּרְמִיו, 'these men were bound… and were thrown', and in 3:23 the men fell into the fire, נְפַלוּ. The sentence adds a passive participle, מְכַפְּתִין, 'bound', which says in what state they fell.

In 3:24 the king is astonished: תְּוַהּ וְקָם, 'he was astonished and rose', two perfects joined by וְ. Then עָנֵה וְאָמַר begins a speech, and the answer to it is told with the plural participles עָנַיִן וְאָמְרִין. In the king's own words (3:25) the participle is the verb of the present: אֲנָה חָזֵה, 'I see'.
So the story moves by perfects for the events, by participles for speech and for what is seen, and by the particles that mark each step.

sections.heading: Marking the steps: אֱדַיִן, בֵּאדַיִן and time phrases
body: אֱדַיִן and בֵּאדַיִן are two spellings of one word, 'then'. They open a new step in the story and usually stand before the subject: בֵּאדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר (3:19), בֵּאדַיִן גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ (3:21), אֱדַיִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא (3:24), בֵּאדַיִן קְרֵב נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר (3:26). In Daniel 3:13 the word appears twice in one verse: first the king commands, and then the men are brought.

Phrases of time do the same work. בֵּהּ זִמְנָא and בַּהּ שַׁעֲתָא mean 'at that time' and 'at that hour' (Daniel 3:7 and 3:6). A phrase like כָּל קֳבֵל דְּנָה, 'therefore', links a new step to the one before: Daniel 3:22 begins with it and then tells how the flame killed the men who had taken the three up to the furnace.
Together these words give Aramaic narrative an order. The word 'then' tells the reader that a new event follows; the verb itself does not.

sections.heading: Aramaic and Hebrew side by side
body: The table below sets forms from the two languages next to each other. Each Hebrew form is a real form from the Hebrew Bible and each Aramaic form is a real form from the Aramaic of the Bible. Several of the differences have already appeared in this course: the ending that makes a noun definite, the לְ that marks an object, the all-purpose word דִּי, and the infinitive that begins with מ.
Do not treat any of these as a rule that works in every verse. Aramaic of the Bible shows both Hebrew-like and Aramaic-like behaviour, and the two languages are close relatives that share much.

misunderstandings: The וְ at the start of an Aramaic clause is not the Hebrew narrative וַ. It only joins; it does not mark time or sequence.
A story with participles is not in the present tense. The setting makes עָנֵה וְאָמַר past; it is the same pair that opens speeches throughout the stories.
אֱדַיִן and בֵּאדַיִן are not different words. They are two spellings, and the בְּ of בֵּאדַיִן does not mean 'in'.
Aramaic does not lack a way to mark the object: it uses לְ, and sometimes the particle יָת with a suffix (יָתְהוֹן in Daniel 3:12). It just does not use the Hebrew word.

deeper.heading: Why compare at all?
body: Aramaic and Hebrew belong to the same wider family and share most of their grammar. Comparing them makes the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra easier to learn and also shows what is distinctive. Scholars use the differences to date texts and to ask how much Aramaic influenced late Hebrew. The comparison in this lesson is meant only as an aid to reading; it settles no question of date or authorship.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then was Nebuchadnezzar filled with fury, and the form of his visage was changed, against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; he spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was wont to be heated.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בֵּאדַיִן, 'then', opens the step. הִתְמְלִי and אֶשְׁתַּנִּי are perfects telling what happened to the king. The pair עָנֵה וְאָמַר, two participles, opens his speech.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then these men were bound in their cloaks, their tunics, and their robes, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: After בֵּאדַיִן two plain perfects, כְּפִתוּ and וּרְמִיו, are joined by וְ. Nothing in the second verb marks it as 'next'; the order of events is the order of the words.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was alarmed, and rose up in haste; he spoke and said unto his ministers: 'Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?' They answered and said unto the king: 'True, O king.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אֱדַיִן is a spelling of 'then'. תְּוַהּ וְקָם are two perfects, 'was astonished and rose'. עָנֵה וְאָמַר opens the king's question, and עָנַיִן וְאָמְרִין, plural participles, open the answer.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace; he spoke and said: 'Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, ye servants of God Most High, come forth, and come hither.' Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, came forth out of the midst of the fire.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בֵּאדַיִן appears twice. The first introduces the king's approach (a perfect, קְרֵב); the second introduces the coming out of the three men (a participle, נָפְקִין). A participle can carry the action after 'then'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spoke and said unto Daniel: 'Thy God whom thou servest continually, He will deliver thee.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בֵּאדַיִן, 'then', opens the step; the king's order is a perfect (אֲמַר), and the men's action וְהַיְתִיו, 'and they brought', is another perfect with וְ. The לְ on לְדָנִיֵּאל marks Daniel as the one brought.

A perfect and an infinitive

The second begins a condition

practice.explain: Aramaic narrative uses 'then' to mark each step. The verse has two steps: the order, and its carrying out.

Perfects of a story
Imperatives
Participles of the present

They are told with ordinary perfects joined by וְ, after the word for 'then'

They are opposites, 'then' and 'now'
They are two spellings of the same word, 'then'
אֱדַיִן means 'then' and בֵּאדַיִן means 'in the judgment'
check.explain: Both introduce the next step of the story. The בְּ is not a preposition here.

options: By the prefix לְ on the name
By a doubled consonant in the name
By the ending -אָ on the name
By the preposition עַל
check.explain: Aramaic often marks a person who is the object with לְ. It is the Aramaic counterpart of the separate object word in Hebrew.

check.prompt: How does Aramaic make מַלְכָּא (word 1) definite, as 'the king'?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.

options: By the word דִּי
By the ending -אָ on the noun
By nothing; there is no way to say 'the'
By a separate word before the noun
check.explain: The determined state ends in -אָ. Hebrew uses a prefix on the noun for the same job.

check.prompt: What is distinctive about the infinitive לְמִבְנֵא (word 9), 'to build'?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Then rose up Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God which is at Jerusalem; and with them were the prophets of God, helping them.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a participle
It ends in -ָה, like the infinitives of the derived stems
It is an imperfect
It has an initial מ after the prefix לְ, as the Peal infinitive does
check.explain: The Peal infinitive adds מ before the root letters (לְמִבְנֵא, לְמִכְנַשׁ). Hebrew has no such מ in its ordinary infinitive.

check.prompt: What does the וְ at the beginning of וְגֻבְרַיָּא (word 0) do?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, fell down bound into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It means 'then'
It joins the sentence to the previous one, without saying that one thing followed another
It changes the perfect into a future
It makes the verb a narrative form
check.explain: Aramaic וְ is a simple link. The order of the story comes from the sequence of the words and from אֱדַיִן and בֵּאדַיִן.

check.prompt: What does כָּל קֳבֵל דְּנָה (words 0 to 2) do at the start of this verse?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Therefore because the king's commandment was peremptory, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It means 'because' and introduces the reason for the earlier events
It begins a condition
It introduces a direct quotation
It means 'therefore' and links the new step to what has just been told
check.explain: With דְּנָה, 'this', the phrase means 'for this reason'. It joins the story of the furnace's heat to the order that was given.

check.prompt: Which statement about Aramaic and Hebrew narrative is right?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said unto them: 'Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, that ye serve not my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Aramaic tells stories with the wayyiqtol, as Hebrew does
Aramaic has no consecutive forms and tells its stories with ordinary perfects and participles, using words like 'then'
Aramaic tells stories only with the imperfect
Aramaic and Hebrew tell stories in exactly the same way
check.explain: Hebrew has the wayyiqtol. The pair עָנֵה וְאָמַר, two participles, is the Aramaic counterpart.

reading.why: The furnace story: the king's fury, the order, the throwing, his astonishment and his question. It shows the whole method: perfects for events, participles for speech and for what is seen, and בֵּאדַיִן and אֱדַיִן to mark the steps, all without a consecutive form.
